newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong political parties at a glance.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong political parties at a glance.

text.p: The British colony of Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule on July 1. Here are sketches of the major political formations in the territory.

DEMOCRATIC PARTY -- The largest and most popular party in Hong Kong, led by lawyer Martin Lee. It was formed in October 1994 after a merger between the United Democrats of Hong Kong and the Meeting Point. The Democratic Party holds 19 seats in the 60-seat elected Legislative Council. It is also the loudest voice in Hong Kong's democracy movement. The Democrats oppose the controversial Provisional Legislature established by China and refused to take part in it. However, they vow to run in the first post-handover election, which is expected to be held in the first half of 1998. The Democratic Party is viewed by Beijing as "subversive".

LIBERAL PARTY -- A party of business tycoons established in July 1993. It was formed to counter the United Democrats of Hong Kong, forerunners of the Democratic Party, in the Legislative Council. It held 15 seats at the time. But in the 1995 election staged under Governor Chris Patten's electoral reforms, it lost its place as the largest political group in the council to the Democratic Party. Its chairman Allen Lee, who was running in a rural and conservative district, is the only Liberal elected by direct vote. Its nine other legislators in the council were chosen to represent their respective professional sectors, holding safe seats in these "functional constituencies". The Liberals also have 10 seats in the Provisional Legislature.

DEMOCRATIC ALLIANCE FOR THE BETTERMENT OF HONG KONG -- A pro-Beijing party with its roots in the labour movement. It was formed in July 1992. With seven seats in the Legislative Council it is the largest pro-China party. For the DAB, the 1995 poll was a disaster. Its leaders Tsang Yok-sing, Tam Yiu-chung and Cheng Kai-nam were rejected by voters in favour of Democrats. But their patriotism is now being rewarded by China. The three, along with seven other DAB members, have seats in the Provisional Legislature. Despite political differences with the Democrats, the two sides sometimes agree when it comes to social issues.

ASSOCIATION FOR DEMOCRACY AND PEOPLE'S LIVELIHOOD -- One of the oldest interest groups in Hong Kong. Although it has four members in the Legislative Council, it does not call itself a political party. The ADPL was formed in August 1986 with the aim of broadening democracy and improving the welfare of Hong Kong's people. But in recent years, the group has softened its stance on democracy in Hong Kong under Chinese rule. The ADPL defends its position by saying dialogue with Beijing is more constructive than confrontation. The four ADPL legislators have also been appointed to the Provisional Legislature.

LIBERAL DEMOCRATIC FOUNDATION -- The second-oldest pro-China political party in Hong Kong. It was formed in November 1990. It is less popular than the DAB. Its members are predominantly from the business and professional sectors. Although party members such as Maria Tam and Raymond Wu are highly trusted by Beijing, they are not as popular with the Hong Kong public. There has been talk that the LDF will merge with the Hong Kong Progressive Alliance, another small pro-China party, ahead of the 1998 election. The new party is likely to be called the Hong Kong Progressive Alliance. The LDF has only one member in the Legislative Council, but three in the Provisional Legislature.

HONG KONG PROGRESSIVE ALLIANCE -- A pro-China party formed in July 1994. Its members, like the LDF, are mainly from the business and professional sectors. The party, led by former Law Society president Ambrose Lau is highly trusted by Beijing. It has five members in the Provisional Legislature but only one representative in the elected Legislative Council. And that seat, held by Lau himself, is not a directly elected position. The party has proposed changing the electoral system from first-past-the-post to multi-seat, single-vote after the handover. Analysts say this would give the party a better chance of securing seats in the council, to the detriment of the Democratic Party.

THE FRONTIER -- A political grouping set up in August 1996 by five independent legislators including vocal pro-democracy activist Emily Lau. The group aims to strengthen the territory's democracy movement. It is more aggressive than the Democratic Party in its opposition to China's plans to curb civil and political liberties and install the Provisional Legislature. Frontier members led the charge protesting outside the Hong Kong Convention Centre when a China-assembled committee chose the territory's post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa in December 1996. They were dragged away by police.

NEW HONG KONG ALLIANCE -- The oldest pro-China political party in Hong Kong. It was formed in May 1989. The party's stand is similar to the LDF and the Progressive Alliance. It is a minor political party on the territory's political scene, but its members are trusted by Chinese authorities. Philip Wong is the only core member sitting in the Legislative Council. He was appointed by China to join a team of experts on the 1997/98 transition year budget in the Sino-British Joint Liaison Group. Another core member, Kan Fook-yee, is a local deputy to China's parliament, the National People's Congress. These two are the party's only members in the Provisional Legislature.

123 DEMOCRATIC ALLIANCE -- The only pro-Taiwan party in Hong Kong. It is a fringe group. Only its chairman Lawrence Yam holds a seat in the Legislative Council. But the party knows how to attract media attention. In the first meeting of the Legislative Council after the 1995 election, Yam made a show of pledging his loyalty to a portrait of Sun Yat-sen, the father of China's first republic, outside the council building.

CITIZENS PARTY -- Prominent independent legislator Christine Loh launched the new party on May 4 this year. Apart from her none of the 14 founding members have experience in public service. Although Loh is a major political personality, her party is unlikely to play a major part in the first Legislative Council election under Chinese rule in 1998. The new party advocates universal suffrage in Hong Kong and free-market economics allied with environmentally-friendly policies.
